title: People who cannot manage their thirst. Part 3
scripture_text: ‘’The Pharisees heard the crowd whispering such things about him. Then the Chief Priests and the Pharisees sent temple guards to arrest him. Jesus said “I am with you for only a short time and then I am going to the one who sent me. You will look for me, but you will not find me; and where I am, you cannot come.” The Jews said to one another, “Where does this man intend to go that we cannot find him? Will he go where our people live scattered among the Greeks, and teach the Greeks? What did he mean when he said, ‘You will look for me, but you will not find me,’ and ‘Where I am, you cannot come’?”
devotional:
On the last and greatest day of the festival, Jesus stood and said in a loud voice, “Let anyone who is thirsty come to me and drink. Whoever believes in me, as Scripture has said, rivers of living water will flow from within them.” By this he meant the Spirit whom those who believed in him were later to receive. Up to that time the Spirit had not been given, since Jesus had not yet been glorified. On hearing his words, some of the people said, “Surely this man is the Prophet.” Others said, “He is the Messiah.” Still others asked, “How can the Messiah come from Galilee? Does not Scripture say that the Messiah will come from David’s descendants and from Bethlehem the town where David lived?” Thus the people were divided because of Jesus. Some wanted to seize him, but no one laid a hand on him. Finally the temple guards went back to the chief priests and the Pharisees, who asked them, “Why didn’t you bring him in?” “No one ever spoke the way this man does,” the guards replied. “You mean he has deceived you also?” the Pharisees retorted.“Have any of the rulers or of the Pharisees believed in him? No! But this mob that knows nothing of the law—there is a curse on them.”

The Jews in Jerusalem thought that Jesus was going to the Diaspora, who are the Jews who were dispersed among the Greek world. “Where does this man intend to go that we cannot find him? Will he go where our people live scattered among the Greeks, and teach the Greeks?’ John 7:35.

To them it seemed that since Jesus couldn’t crack the strictest of Jews living in the heart of Israel, he was going to give up on them and try to influence the less informed and the less committed Jews in the Greek speaking world. They misunderstood what he was saying; they saw this as a defeat for Jesus. They saw this as a way for Jesus to continue His ministry without the threat of the Jewish leaders who lived in Jerusalem.

This incident gives us some insight into misunderstanding and how it works.

These people did a number of things that compounded their misunderstanding.

(1) They assumed that they understood what Jesus meant when he said "I am going to be with you just a little while longer and then I will go away to him who sent me. You will seek for me but you will not find me, and where I am you cannot come"

(2) They didn’t listen properly to what Jesus said. When they quoted Jesus they said ‘what does he mean when he said, you will look for me, but you will not find me, and where I am you cannot come?’ They left out "I am going to be with you just a little while longer and then I will go away to him who sent me.” If they had listened to all that Jesus said, and thought about it, they would have been unable to come to the conclusions they did, because Jesus said, ‘then I will go away to him who sent me,’ not to the Jews in the diaspora.

Listening to others means that we choose to hear all they have got to say, and not jump to our own conclusions.

(3) John says, ‘The Jews said to one another.’ They didn’t bring their questions to Jesus, but discussed Him amongst themselves. When people begin to discuss misunderstandings instead of going to the right source where they can be addressed, they become more inclined to believe fiction over fact. At this time though, Jesus did not correct their misunderstanding.

These guards heard someone speak with love.

‘On the last and greatest day of the feast Jesus stood and said in a loud voice, ‘if anyone is thirsty let him come to me and drink.’

John 7:37.Before we look in detail at what Jesus says here we need to mention a few things

The vulnerability of Jesus’ invitation.

When we consider the events of this day, it’s important to remember that Jesus, far from turning himself away from the multitudes, many of whom had rejected him, He extended his gracious invitation: ‘If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink.’

This invitation was to the very same people who had been hostile, disbelieving and dismissive of him.

As the guards sent to arrest Him, heard Jesus speak, they not only heard his words, but they also felt his love. The lack of love in our hearts, even for our enemies, will render our words as superficial and useless. Despite the hatred of the people around him, Jesus knew that there were some who had a genuine thirst for God, and Jesus was prepared to open up his life to them.

The timing of the invitation.

It was on the last day of the feast, the day when people were leaving after a week of religious activity. Surly this was the worst time to make such an invitation, or maybe not. People had just experienced the effects that legalistic religion had done to the Jewish religion. It would have been difficult to be spiritually refreshed in Jerusalem at this time because of the hatred and bitterness of the religious authorities. So to prevent people from going away thirsty, Jesus gives this invitation.

The immediate context

There were two important ceremonies that were part of ‘The Feast of Tabernacles' celebration during Jesus' time that are especially important in the context of John 7 and 8. The first involved water and the second involved light. Because The Feast of Tabernacles was an autumn agricultural festival, special prayers for rain were made during the celebration. If rain fell at the time of Tabernacles or shortly afterwards, it was seen as an indication of forthcoming ample rains that would prepare and restore the soil for a successful crop the following year. Zechariah 10:1 contains instructions to pray for rain. Zechariah 14:17 warns that rain will be withheld if the Tabernacles’ ceremony is not properly celebrated.

In the I.V.P New Testament commentary on John’s Gospel, Murray writes:

‘It is virtually certain that the passage assumes the rite of water-drawing that took place on each of the seven days of the festival proper. The pilgrims entered into the procedures with greatest delight; it is stated, “He who has not seen the joy of the water-drawing has not seen joy in his whole lifetime.” At the break of day priests processed from the temple to the pool of Siloam. There they filled a golden pitcher with water and bore it back to the temple. On approaching the Watergate on the south side of the inner court a trumpet was sounded three times—joyous blasts which were explicitly related to Isa 12:3, “With joy you will draw water from the wells of salvation.” The priests bearing the water then processed around the altar, watched by the pilgrims, while the temple choir sang the Hallel (i.e., Pss 113–18). When the opening words of Psalm 118 were reached, “Give thanks to the Lord,” every man and boy shook the lulab (a bunch of willow and myrtle tied with palm) with his right hand and held aloft citrus fruit in his left hand (a sign of the harvest gathered in), and the cry “Give thanks to the Lord” was repeated three times.’

‘This invitation to come and drink is the climax of a series of references to water in this Gospel: the water turned to wine (chap. 2), the water of the new birth (chap. 3), the living water (chap. 4), the cleansing water of Bethesda (chap. 5) and the calming of the waters (chap. 6). All of these have revealed Jesus as the agent of God who brings God's gracious offer of life.’
prayer: Father thank you for the very kind invitation of Jesus.
